prompt.context: Our client, Tarrant Fixtures, is a low-intensity manufacturing company that produces display fixtures for retail clients. The company's financial performance has deteriorated in each of the last three years. Specifically, they are concerned with the company's falling Return on Investment (ROI).
prompt.question: The CEO has asked us to look into this problem. How can Tarrant Fixtures get back on track?

clarifying_info.q: What types of products does Tarrant Fixtures sell?
clarifying_info.a: Two types: Custom displays (50% of sales) — produced only when an order is placed and payment is received. Standard displays (50% of sales) — manufactured to open standard for display sizes/types and stored in inventory (built-to-stock). 5 standardized products account for 80% of sales in standardized products; the number of standardized products increased from 5 to 12 over the last 3 years.

clarifying_info.q: What has happened to revenues over the past three years?
clarifying_info.a: Total revenues grew by 25%, from $100M to $125M, equally across both product types.
Costs of production (COGS, labor, SG&A, etc.) remained stable as a percentage of revenue at 80%.

clarifying_info.q: Has the company made any new capital investments?
clarifying_info.a: No. The company has no new investments in Property, Plant, & Equipment (CAPEX = $0).

clarifying_info.q: What has happened to working capital?
clarifying_info.a: Total Working Capital Employed three years ago was $80M; today it is $130M. Inventory levels increased by 200% (primarily in finished goods), from $25M to $75M.
The market has grown 25% in total over the past three years.
The client has remained the industry market share leader in displays and has maintained 25% market share over the past three years.

clarifying_info.q: What is the competitive environment like?
clarifying_info.a: There are several players in the market, but everything has remained stable from a competitive standpoint.

framework: Define ROI: ROI = Net Profit / Capital Employed. Decompose into numerator (Net Profit) and denominator (Capital Employed).
Analyze Net Profit: Revenue trends, cost structure (COGS, SG&A as % of revenue), absolute profit levels over three years.
Analyze Capital Employed: Break down into PP&E, Working Capital (Inventory, AR, AP, Cash). Identify which component has changed.
Identify root cause of capital increase: Drill into inventory build-up — which product lines, why inventory grew, demand forecasting accuracy.
Recommend fixes to reduce inventory and improve ROI: Portfolio rationalization, demand forecasting, inventory write-offs.

questions.prompt: Define ROI and identify where the problem might lie.
questions.guidance: Candidate must know the ROI formula: ROI = Net Profit / Capital Employed. They should split the analysis into the numerator (profit) and denominator (capital employed) and propose examining each for deterioration.

questions.prompt: Calculate Net Profit for Year 1 and Year 3. Is profit the cause of falling ROI?
questions.guidance: Net Profit = Revenue - Cost of Production. Show that profits grew 25% in line with revenue, so the numerator is not the problem. The issue must be in Capital Employed.

math.setup: Net Profit = Revenue × (1 - Cost %). Year 1: $100M × 20% = $20M. Year 3: $125M × 20% = $25M.
steps: Profit grew 25%, matching revenue growth — not the cause of ROI decline
math.answer: Net Profit grew from $20M to $25M (+25%). Profit is NOT the cause of the ROI problem.

questions.prompt: Examine Capital Employed. What changed and why?
questions.guidance: A line-by-line walkthrough of the Working Capital statement should reveal: PP&E is constant (no CAPEX), AR/AP/Cash are stable, but Inventory increased by $50M (from $25M to $75M). Total Working Capital rose from $80M to $130M — entirely driven by inventory. Candidate should calculate the ROI decline.

math.setup: ROI = Net Profit / Capital Employed. Year 1: $20M / $80M. Year 3: $25M / $130M.
steps: Working Capital increased $50M, all from Inventory ($25M → $75M)
PP&E, AR, AP, Cash all stable
math.answer: ROI fell from 25% to ~19.2%. The entire $50M increase in Capital Employed came from Inventory build-up.

questions.prompt: What are the likely causes of the inventory increase?
questions.guidance: Strong answers identify: (1) proliferation of standardized product lines — SKUs grew from 5 to 12 while top 5 still drive 80% of sales; (2) inaccurate demand forecasts leading to excess safety stock; (3) obsolete inventories of outdated/slow-moving product lines.

questions.prompt: What should management do to fix the inventory problem?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recommend: writing off or working down obsolete inventory (noting this causes an immediate profit hit, so management may resist); improving demand forecasting to set realistic safety stock levels; rationalizing the standard product line back to the top 5 products (which represent 80% of standardized sales).

brainstorming.prompt: What actions can Tarrant Fixtures take to reduce its inventory and improve ROI?

categories.name: Portfolio Rationalization
ideas: Reduce standardized product SKUs from 12 back to the top 5 products that drive 80% of sales
Discontinue slow-moving or unprofitable SKU variants
Implement a formal SKU approval process to limit future proliferation

categories.name: Demand Forecasting
ideas: Use historical sales data to set evidence-based safety stock levels
Collaborate with retail clients for demand visibility (VMI/consignment)
Reduce lead times to lower required safety stock buffers

categories.name: Inventory Write-down / Liquidation
ideas: Write off obsolete finished goods inventory
Work with clients on promotions to sell through excess inventory

categories.name: Production Policy
ideas: Shift more products from build-to-stock to build-to-order where feasible
Reduce batch sizes to lower average inventory levels
Improve production scheduling to reduce WIP and finished goods buffers

recommendation: Tarrant Fixtures' ROI has fallen from 25% to ~19% over three years due to a $50M increase in inventory-driven Working Capital, not from deteriorating profits (which grew 25% in line with revenue).
The root cause is the proliferation of standardized product SKUs from 5 to 12, combined with inaccurate demand forecasting, resulting in excess and potentially obsolete finished goods inventory.

We recommend the client immediately rationalize its standard product portfolio back to the core 5 SKUs representing 80% of standardized sales, write off or liquidate obsolete inventory, and implement improved demand forecasting.
risks: Writing off obsolete inventory will cause an immediate one-time hit to profits, which management may be reluctant to accept.
Reducing the product line could risk losing some customers who order the discontinued SKUs.
Improving demand forecasting requires investment and organizational change that takes time to yield results.
next_steps: Conduct a full SKU-level profitability analysis to confirm which 7 standardized products to discontinue.
Quantify the obsolete inventory write-off amount and model the P&L impact.
Evaluate demand forecasting software options and estimate implementation timeline and cost.
Develop a communication plan for retail clients affected by SKU discontinuation.
